analysisPurpose: Assess changes in hub-height wind speed and wind-energy potential from the past to the future.
analysisTechnique: Regional ensemble analysis, linear trends, and load-factor calculation
analysisMethodDescription: The trained Random Forest model was applied to Euro-CORDEX projections, and 10 models whose monthly mean w100 distributions were consistent with ERA5 under a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test at α = 0.1 were selected for trend analysis.
analysisKeyOutcome: European w100 showed a significant decreasing ensemble-mean trend of -0.019 m s−1 decade−1 during 1979–2019, and the decreasing trend increased along the 21st century under RCP8.5.

analysisPurpose: Group monitoring stations with relatively homogeneous wind-speed behavior and similar numbers of components.
analysisMethodDescription: Ward's method was applied at a similarity level of 21.09 and a Euclidean distance of 0.79, separating the 27 stations into four groups.
analysisKeyOutcome: Four station groups were produced and used to separate calibration series from series used for method-accuracy analysis.

analysisPurpose: Assess variation of Weibull shape and scale parameters with height above ground level.
analysisTechnique: Extrapolation from 10 m to 50 m, 100 m, 200 m, and 300 m
analysisKeyOutcome: The shape factor decreased and the scale factor increased with height under the extrapolation methodology.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind-energy potential at Catalca using annual average wind power density and Weibull analysis.
analysisTechnique: Wind-speed extrapolation, Weibull distribution fitting, and wind power density calculation
analysisMethodDescription: Measured wind speeds at 10 m were extrapolated to 30, 60, and 80 m before annual power densities and Weibull parameters were evaluated.
analysisKeyOutcome: The authors report that the annual average power densities prove the site's suitability for wind power generation.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind characteristics and wind-energy potential at Tehran using long-term meteorological measurements.
analysisTechnique: Statistical analysis, Weibull distribution fitting, wind power and energy density calculation, and wind rose analysis
analysisMethodDescription: Three-hourly wind measurements from 1995–2005 were processed to obtain mean wind speeds, standard deviations, Weibull parameters, characteristic wind speeds, wind power density, wind energy density, and wind-direction frequencies.
analysisKeyOutcome: The site was not considered suitable for large-scale wind-electric application under current conditions, but may support small-scale non-grid-connected uses.

analysisPurpose: Characterize wind speed, wind direction, Weibull distribution, turbulence, power density, and energy potential.
analysisTechnique: descriptive statistics, Weibull fitting, wind roses, wind-duration curves, and power-density calculation
analysisMethodDescription: Measured and extrapolated wind data were statistically analyzed at multiple heights and sites.
analysisKeyOutcome: Damghan had the best conditions among the five towns, while Moalleman was the best of the detailed sites.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind-energy potential in Zahedan.
analysisTechnique: Two-parameter Weibull distribution analysis using the standard deviation method.
analysisKeyOutcome: The five-year average wind power density was 89.184 W/m2 and the average wind energy density was 781.252 kWh/m2.

analysisPurpose: Evaluate wind energy potential and assess the simulated performance of commercial wind turbines and wind-powered pumps at three sites.
analysisTechnique: Weibull distribution analysis, hub-height extrapolation, wind-turbine performance calculation, and Rayleigh-based pump simulation
analysisMethodDescription: Monthly wind-speed data were analysed using the two-parameter Weibull distribution. Wind speeds were adjusted to hub height using a power law, and turbine energy output, capacity factor, and water-pumping output were calculated.
analysisKeyOutcome: Enugu had the highest wind-energy indicators among the three sites, while all sites were reported to have strong potential for water pumping.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind characteristics and offshore wind energy potential at three offshore locations surrounding Hong Kong.
analysisTechnique: Wind-speed adjustment by power-law approximation; Weibull distribution fitting; calculation of wind power density, operating probability, most probable wind speed, and wind speed carrying maximum energy.
analysisKeyOutcome: The southeastern waters near Waglan Island were identified as the most promising location for offshore wind-farm development in Hong Kong.

analysisPurpose: To quantify uncertainty in annual energy production caused by variability of natural wind and power performance.
analysisMethodDescription: Probability distributions for the dominant AEP-influencing variables are sampled and combined to generate annual energy production values.
analysisKeyOutcome: The standard deviation of generated AEP normalized by its average value was 11% in the Kwangyang Bay case study.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind-speed distributions, wind power density, and wind-energy potential at the five selected locations.
analysisTechnique: Weibull probability density function and wind-speed extrapolation

analysisPurpose: To provide a combined view of the distribution of wind velocity and wind direction at the studied site.
analysisMethodDescription: The wind rose was constructed using wind-speed data measured at 10-minute intervals and wind-direction data at a height of 50 m.
analysisKeyOutcome: Most of the wind blows from the East and the Northeast, represented by sectors 3 and 4. These sectors represent 31.17% of all wind speeds in all sectors.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind characteristics and potential wind energy at five typical sites in Hong Kong.
analysisTechnique: Weibull distribution fitting, wind-speed extrapolation, operating-probability calculation, and wind-power-density calculation.
analysisMethodDescription: One-minute wind data were transformed to hourly mean wind speed. Wind speeds were transformed to 80 m hub height using a power law, and Weibull parameters were estimated by moment, maximum-likelihood, and power-density methods.
analysisKeyOutcome: Hilltops and offshore islands were identified as the most promising locations for wind-energy exploitation in Hong Kong.

analysisPurpose: To show wind direction and the resultant of the wind-speed direction.
analysisMethodDescription: Observed wind-speed frequencies were plotted in polar diagrams with respect to cardinal points. The 360-degree cycle was divided into 16 sectors, each covering an arc of 22.5 degrees.
analysisKeyOutcome: The most probable wind directions blowing from were 190 degrees at Kudat and 269 degrees at Labuan through the study years.

analysisPurpose: Evaluate area-specific wind-resource characteristics and produce estimates of wind speed at various distances from the measuring mast.
analysisKeyOutcome: The lowest average wind speed was 2.66 m/s and the highest was 5.56 m/s extrapolated at 78 m from ground level. The authors concluded that profitable turbines would need to be installed near the mast on the north-east side of the map.

analysisName: Wind-energy integration and agricultural pumping-demand analysis
analysisPurpose: Estimate agricultural irrigation-pump demand that could be met through wind-farm energy subject to alternative curtailment rates and wind-farm layouts.
analysisMethodDescription: Six wind-farm layouts, WF1 through WF6, containing six to one wind turbines, respectively, were examined under six curtailment rates, yielding 36 scenarios.
analysisKeyOutcome: WF4, with three wind turbines, was recommended as the final wind-farm configuration when system, environmental, and independent-power-producer perspectives were considered together.

analysisPurpose: Evaluate the distribution of wind direction and the frequency of wind speed in particular directions.
analysisMethodDescription: Wind-direction data were plotted in polar wind-rose diagrams using Windographer software. Each wind rose diagram consisted of 16 sectors, each covering an arc of 22.5°.
analysisKeyOutcome: The most frequent wind direction was from the north in Bordkhun; for all sites investigated, the weakest and less frequent wind direction was from the east.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind characteristics, wind power density, capacity factors, and annual turbine output energy at six Moroccan coastal sites.
analysisTechnique: Weibull distribution fitting using least squares, maximum likelihood, and WAsP methods
analysisMethodDescription: Wind-speed frequency distributions were compared with actual wind data using R2; wind power density, net capacity factor, and turbine output energy were evaluated.

analysisPurpose: Characterize wind speed and direction and assess wind energy potential at Bohai Bay.
analysisMethodDescription: Wind data were analyzed at seasonal, monthly, and hourly timescales; Weibull, Nakagami, Rician, and Rayleigh distributions were fitted using nonlinear least-squares methods.
analysisKeyOutcome: Nakagami distribution performed best for forecasting wind power density according to error-sum values.

analysisPurpose: To assess wind characteristics and wind power potential in the capital city of Chad.
analysisKeyOutcome: The site was concluded to be suitable only for small-scale applications.

analysisPurpose: Evaluate wind characteristics and wind potential at Ain Salah.
analysisTechnique: Weibull distribution fitting and wind-rose analysis
analysisMethodDescription: Wind speed and direction data recorded every three hours over the reported 10-year period were statistically analyzed; Weibull parameters were determined using the standard deviation method.
analysisKeyOutcome: The reported Weibull parameters were k = 2.48 and C = 6.0 m/s, and the annual mean wind speed was 5.4 m/s at 10 m.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind energy potential and wind characteristics across Eritrea's coastal region, western lowlands, and central highlands.
analysisTechnique: Analysis of measured wind time series, Weibull fitting, wind-speed extrapolation, wind power-density calculation, and comparison with Global Wind Atlas values.
analysisKeyOutcome: The best studied wind sites were found in the southern coastal area near the mouth of the Red Sea, with good sites also found in the central highlands.

analysisPurpose: To assess wind power potential in Jeddah using meteorological wind data.
analysisTechnique: Monthly, annual and hourly wind-speed analysis with Weibull-distribution fitting.
analysisMethodDescription: Monthly mean wind speeds and standard deviations were analyzed; annual Weibull shape and scale parameters were obtained and compared with measured wind-speed values.
analysisKeyOutcome: Average wind speed was reported as insufficient for large-size wind turbines, while the region was considered suitable for small-scale off-grid wind applications.

analysisPurpose: To determine the most probable wind direction over the eleven-year period.
analysisTechnique: Polar diagrams with 16 directional sectors of 22.5 degrees.
analysisMethodDescription: Wind-direction frequencies were plotted with respect to cardinal points.
analysisKeyOutcome: The paper reports the most probable wind direction as 315 degrees, described by the authors as SE winds; it also reports SE and ESE at 315 degrees and 337.5 degrees, respectively.

analysisPurpose: Characterize the recorded wind-speed data before probability-density-function fitting.
analysisTechnique: Arithmetic mean, variance, standard deviation, standard error, skewness, kurtosis, calm frequency, and absent-data fraction.

analysisPurpose: Investigate spatial correlation and spatial dependence of wind power before spatial prediction.
analysisTechnique: Fitted semivariogram models assessed using mean square error and subjective comparison with theoretical semivariogram shape.
analysisKeyOutcome: The linear semivariogram was selected, but the authors concluded that it could not adequately fit the data and that wind power lacked clear spatial correlation.

analysisPurpose: Create maps representing the spatial trend of wind power in Malaysia.
analysisKeyOutcome: The maps indicated higher wind-power potential in northeast, northwest, and southeast Peninsular Malaysia and in southern Sabah.

analysisPurpose: Evaluate mean wind energy density, mean effective wind energy density, and wind turbine generator capacity factor in order to assess wind sites and candidate wind turbine generators.
analysisTechnique: Use the MKD-estimated wind speed probability distribution, power-law wind-speed extrapolation, and wind turbine generator power-output equations.
analysisKeyOutcome: WTG5 presented the largest annual and seasonal wind-energy assessment indices among the tested WTGs, and the annual and seasonal indices of WTG5 at WF1 were the largest among WTG5 results at the other wind sites.

analysisPurpose: Estimate wind-speed variation with height and wind speed at 80 m.
analysisTechnique: Power Law method and Logarithmic Law.

analysisPurpose: Assess turbulence-intensity variation and its directional distribution at the site.
analysisTechnique: Calculation of turbulence intensity as the ratio of wind-speed standard deviation to mean wind speed and directional polar-diagram analysis.

analysisPurpose: Analyze and predict extreme wind-speed events and estimate the 50-year return-period wind speed.
analysisTechnique: Periodic maxima method, Gumbel distribution, and Harris algorithm.

analysisPurpose: Assess mean wind speed spatial variability, seasonal directional characteristics, and diurnal wind speed variability.
Estimate wind power density by wind speed and wind direction after selecting the best bivariate wind model.
analysisTechnique: Application of the fitted bivariate joint probability density in the wind power density equation.
analysisKeyOutcome: Detailed wind-power-density distributions were estimated for Andros, Pylos, and Mar de Alboran.

analysisPurpose: Assess offshore wind-energy potential using fitted wind-speed distributions and indices including availability factor, capacity factor and turbine efficiency.
Estimate extreme wind speeds and associated potential risks for specified return periods.
analysisTechnique: GH re-analysis followed by Gumbel and GEV distribution fitting

analysisPurpose: Examine whether the wind-speed distributions change in the long term.
analysisTechnique: Mann–Whitney U test and two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test
analysisKeyOutcome: The mutation tests indicate that wind-speed distributions at all four sites do not change.

analysisPurpose: Calculate cumulative distribution functions, mean wind energy density, mean effective wind energy density, and the mode of wind power density distribution from DKDM probability densities.
analysisTechnique: Numerical integration of probability-density values calculated at specific grid points by inverse discrete cosine transformation.

analysisPurpose: Evaluate sensitivity of four wind-speed distribution functions to measurement-data accuracy.
analysisTechnique: Comparison of nine goodness-of-fit indices for actual and truncated data using MOM and MLE.
analysisKeyOutcome: Lognormal fitted actual data best, whereas Weibull-MLE was generally preferred for truncated data.

analysisPurpose: Estimate wind power density, wind energy density, most probable wind speed, and maximum energy carrying wind speed from fitted wind-speed distributions.
Assess and map wind-energy potential in the Far North Region of Cameroon.
analysisTechnique: Wind-speed distribution fitting, wind-speed extrapolation, and wind-power-density estimation
analysisMethodDescription: The assessment uses Weibull distribution fitting and vertical extrapolation of wind speed.

analysisPurpose: Evaluate the wind-energy resource potential in Ambam.
analysisTechnique: Weibull distribution fitting and wind power density estimation
analysisMethodDescription: Four numerical methods were used to estimate Weibull parameters, and their performances were evaluated using RMSE, chi-square, and R2.
analysisKeyOutcome: Ambam was characterized as an unfavorable site for effective wind-energy production based on the assessed mean wind speed and wind power density.

analysisPurpose: Compare wind speeds and wind power densities in wet and dry seasons.
analysisTechnique: Seasonal partitioning and comparison of wind-speed distributions and power densities
analysisMethodDescription: Five dry-season months from November to March and five wet-season months from May to September were analysed over the 29-year period; April and October were not included.
analysisKeyOutcome: The authors report higher wind speed and higher power density in the wet season than in the dry season.

analysisPurpose: Determine wind directions, wind-speed classes, and mean wind speeds per class for selected periods and durations.
analysisMethodDescription: Wind-speed and direction pairs from the five daily periods were sequentially appended through days, weeks, months, years, and the continuous seven-year period before applying the wind rose Matlab program.
analysisKeyOutcome: All significant winds fell in the first quadrant (NE), predominantly at 10 degrees, with some discernible winds at 20 degrees and 30 degrees.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind-energy potential and investigate wind properties at Alasaba.
analysisTechnique: Weibull probability-distribution fitting and coefficient-of-determination goodness-of-fit testing
analysisMethodDescription: Measured monthly wind-speed distributions were compared with Weibull approximations, and wind power and energy densities were estimated at different heights.

analysisPurpose: Determine wind characteristics and wind energy potential at the selected campus location.
analysisTechnique: Statistical distribution fitting using Weibull and Rayleigh distributions, Moment and Maximum Likelihood parameter estimation, and goodness-of-fit testing.
analysisKeyOutcome: Rayleigh MLE was estimated as the most suitable model among the statistical distributions examined.

analysisPurpose: Determine Weibull parameters, mean wind speed, and mean wind power density for monthly, seasonal, and annual wind-resource analysis.
analysisTechnique: Weibull statistics using the maximum likelihood method
analysisMethodDescription: The Weibull function was employed for wind-data analysis, and its parameters were estimated using the maximum likelihood method.
analysisKeyOutcome: Illizi had higher reported wind speeds and mean power densities than Es senia among the reported monthly values.

analysisPurpose: Assess the wind potential, direction, and frequency of the Laayoune site.
analysisMethodDescription: Processing and analysis of station data from Laayoune over 369 days.

analysisPurpose: To compare wind-speed trends.
analysisTechnique: Modified Mann–Kendall test for serially correlated data using the Hamed and Rao variance correction approach

analysisPurpose: Select suitable areas for a wind farm by extrapolating wind resource over the study area.
analysisTechnique: Wind-resource extrapolation using a generated topographic map and WAsP software
analysisMethodDescription: A wind resource extrapolation was performed using the generated topographic map and WAsP software; wind speed distributions were predicted over the whole area.
analysisKeyOutcome: The resource was reported as relatively high along hill crests, particularly over the big hill east of the data collection site, while it was low around the data collection site and in lower-elevation northern and north-eastern areas.

analysisPurpose: To understand the factors that influence wind power production at Taïba Ndiaye.
analysisTechnique: Annual, monthly, daily, hourly, and intra-day evaluation of production data and comparison with wind conditions at 100 m above ground level.
analysisKeyOutcome: Wind-farm production exhibited seasonal and diurnal variation and a positive correlation with 100 m wind speed.

analysisPurpose: Assess the direction from which wind blows and characterize dominant wind direction at Ziguinchor.
analysisKeyOutcome: For annual 2016–2018 data at 10 m, the dominant wind direction was NNW for ERA5 data and WNW for station data. In spring, the prevailing direction was NW, with maximum occurrence frequencies of 18% and 14% for station and ERA5 data, respectively.

analysisPurpose: Characterize wind regularity in Senegal on a seasonal time scale.
analysisKeyOutcome: The turbulence index was stronger during summer and fall than during winter and spring at 10 m and 100 m. Higher values were mainly observed in southern Senegal, while the lowest values were located in coastal areas and the northern part.

analysisPurpose: Analyze wind-speed classes to support selection of a suitable turbine for a site.
analysisTechnique: Seasonal occurrence percentage of wind classes
analysisMethodDescription: The results section defines class 1 as wind speeds between 0 and 5 m/s and class 2 as wind speeds higher than 5 m/s. The conclusion reverses these class descriptions.
analysisKeyOutcome: conflicting_values

analysisPurpose: Assess wind power potential in Kano for efficient energy utilization.
analysisTechnique: Two-parameter Weibull statistical analysis, wind-speed extrapolation, wind power density estimation, energy density estimation, and energy efficiency index calculation.
analysisKeyOutcome: The authors reported that Kano falls under Class 7 of the wind power density class.

analysisPurpose: To avoid possible misleading indications related to yearly variation in weather condition.
analysisTechnique: Checking the overall consistency of the daily, monthly and yearly average climatic parameters.

analysisPurpose: Evaluate wind-energy potential and support evaluation and planning of future wind-energy projects in the northern coastal region.
analysisTechnique: Two-parameter Weibull distribution fitting and linear regression
analysisMethodDescription: Wind-speed data from selected stations were analysed using the two-parameter Weibull probability distribution function; the Weibull parameters were estimated by linear regression of the cumulative Weibull distribution.

analysisPurpose: Calculate daily mean wind speed, standard deviation, most probable wind speed, wind speed at highest energy, and wind power density.
Determine monthly, seasonal, and yearly wind-resource potential for power generation and assess candidate turbine output.
analysisTechnique: Weibull statistical analysis, wind power density estimation, wind-speed extrapolation, and turbine-output calculation
analysisMethodDescription: The analysis used monthly mean wind-speed and wind-direction data from 1984–2013, daily wind-speed data from 2009–2013, a two-parameter Weibull distribution, and turbine power-output and capacity-factor equations.
analysisKeyOutcome: AV 928 had the highest reported average power output among the six turbines, while reported capacity factors were relatively low.

analysisPurpose: Assess offshore wind-energy potential and identify the distribution model that best fits the available wind data.
analysisTechnique: Weibull, Rayleigh and Exponential probability distribution fitting with goodness-of-fit comparison
analysisKeyOutcome: Weibull distribution had the highest reported R2 values and the lowest reported RMSE and chi-square values among the three distributions at the three locations.

analysisPurpose: Determine uncertainty in mean wind speed within the three locations.
analysisMethodDescription: At a 95% confidence level, uncertainty in the mean wind speed within the three locations was determined.
analysisKeyOutcome: The uncertainty in mean wind speed was reported as ±3.

analysisPurpose: To provide a global view of wind-energy resources in Algeria and indicate regions where a significant wind resource may exist.
analysisTechnique: Maps of wind resource and wind power density
analysisMethodDescription: Annual and seasonal maps of wind-energy resources were established for the studied Algerian regions.
analysisKeyOutcome: The maps provide a global view of wind-energy resources in Algeria and clearly indicate regions where a significant wind resource may exist.

analysisPurpose: To analyse statistical information on wind direction for the studied sites.
analysisMethodDescription: Wind roses were presented for Adrar, Algiers, Tindouf, and Tlemcen, and the statistical information of wind direction was used for a directional classification.
analysisKeyOutcome: The dominant wind directions for the studied sites are North and West.

analysisPurpose: To investigate the effects of uncertainty or changes in input parameters on unit electricity cost.
analysisMethodDescription: Sensitivity analysis was carried out for the Polaris 15-50 wind-turbine model in Oshiyie considering unit turbine cost, discount rate, useful life, other initial capital cost, and capacity factor.
analysisKeyOutcome: When capacity factor was improved by 25%, LCOE decreased by 20%, from US$0.06072/kW h to US$0.04858/kW h. Increasing project life from 20 to 25 years decreased LCOE by about 12.47%, from US$0.06072/kW h to US$0.05315/kW h.

analysisPurpose: Obtain wind speed at the selected turbine hub height for output-power analysis.
analysisTechnique: Wind-speed scaling using the log law formula.
analysisKeyOutcome: A wind speed of about 8.79 m/s was obtained after scaling to the turbine hub height.

analysisPurpose: Determine areas showing a compromise between exploitable wind potential and wind-turbine foundation constraints.
analysisMethodDescription: Bathymetric data from GEBCO were considered together with wind potential; bathymetry values between 0 and 250 m were plotted, with attention to water-depth limits for foundations.
analysisKeyOutcome: The region close to the shore represents the best compromise between wind potential viability and foundation complexity.

analysisPurpose: To evaluate wind potential and electricity generation from selected wind turbines at eight sites.
analysisTechnique: Mean wind-speed calculation, Weibull distribution fitting, wind-power-density calculation, hub-height extrapolation, and turbine-output calculation.

analysisPurpose: Provide information on wind-direction frequencies and wind speed.
analysisMethodDescription: Wind rose plots were prepared for the five selected regions at 50 m using wind-speed-frequency and wind-direction data in different speed bins.
analysisKeyOutcome: For Boujdour, Essaouira, and Laayoune, wind direction at 50 m was reported from the north-east with 42% frequency; Tantan had prevailing wind from the north with 39% occurrence.

analysisPurpose: Assess seasonal patterns and variability in wind-speed-related variables.
analysisKeyOutcome: The PCA indicated a discernible monthly seasonal pattern, with Wsmeans positively correlated with the first dimension and mean Rho negatively correlated with the second dimension.

analysisPurpose: Assess temporal complementarity between solar irradiation and wind-related generation.
analysisTechnique: Pearson correlation coefficient and p-value analysis
analysisKeyOutcome: Most months showed negative correlations, whereas June, July, and August had correlations near zero and were reported as not significant in Table 4.

analysisPurpose: Obtain mean wind-speed results for data from 2008 to 2016 and characterize wind conditions.
analysisTechnique: Weibull distribution analysis and descriptive statistical calculation
analysisMethodDescription: Monthly average wind speed was calculated using a simple statistical method; Weibull parameters were calculated using the energy pattern factor method.
analysisKeyOutcome: Monthly Weibull shape parameters ranged from 2.822 to 6.740 and scale parameters ranged from 5.117 to 7.270 m/s.

analysisPurpose: Obtain mean results from wind-speed data from 2008-2016 and characterize wind-speed variation.
analysisTechnique: simple statistical method and Weibull analysis
analysisMethodDescription: Average monthly wind speed data were calculated using a simple statistical method; Weibull distribution parameters, wind power density, and energy density were calculated.
analysisKeyOutcome: Monthly mean wind speed was reported to range from 4.31 to 6.04 m/s at 10 m height.

analysisPurpose: Identify appropriate areas for wind-farm installation.
analysisTechnique: WAsP calculation using a wind atlas, topography, roughness, and obstacle information
analysisKeyOutcome: Resource maps were obtained with a grid resolution of 300 m; the resource was relatively high along hill ridges and especially on the large hill east of the data-collection site.

analysisPurpose: Analyse wind speed through seasons and annual periods for wind-potential assessment.
analysisTechnique: Weibull distribution, graphs and bar charts
analysisMethodDescription: The analysis had seasonal and annual phases; graphs and bar charts were stated as the major tools.

analysisPurpose: Assess the effect of changing hub height on Weibull parameters, probability density curves, wind power density, capacity factor, and cost of energy.
analysisTechnique: Variation of hub height from 10 to 50 m using the power law equation.
analysisMethodDescription: The analysis considered hub heights of 10 to 50 m and examined resulting changes in k, c, wind power density, capacity factor, and cost of energy.
analysisKeyOutcome: Increasing hub height increased k, c, wind power density, and capacity factor, while cost of energy decreased.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind-energy potential and wind-resource suitability at selected Nigerian locations.
analysisTechnique: Weibull distribution fitting and wind power density estimation
analysisKeyOutcome: Ikeja, Jos and Kano were classified as class 7 at 10 m, while P/H was classified as class 3 at 10 m.

analysisPurpose: To select a wind-speed sampling interval for which the null hypothesis of dependence can be accepted at a significance level of 0.05.
analysisTechnique: Box-Cox transformation, Anderson-Darling normality test, autocorrelation coefficients, and Ljung-Box test
analysisMethodDescription: At each iteration the sampling time was increased by one hour, the sample was transformed to achieve normality, the Anderson-Darling statistic was applied, autocorrelation coefficients were determined, and the Ljung-Box test was applied.
analysisKeyOutcome: The selected data acquisition interval indicating independence was 174 h. For this interval, the sample size n was 300, the effective number of observations N_e was 719, the Box-Cox transformation parameters were b = 1 and k = 0.75, the Anderson-Darling statistics were A_mn = 0.462 and A_cn = 0.752, and the Ljung-Box statistics were Q = 84.52 and Q_c = 90.5 with 70 degrees of freedom.

analysisPurpose: Analyse temporal distribution and prevailing wind directions at the study location.
analysisMethodDescription: Wind rose diagrams with 36 evenly spaced sectors were drawn for each season and for the whole 2005–2021 study period.
analysisKeyOutcome: West was the most prevailing direction during 2005–2021, while north had the lowest occurrence rate.

analysisPurpose: Present frequencies of wind direction for each wind speed at each station.
analysisKeyOutcome: On monthly average, wind flows from South and Southeast in Rwanda, except at Ruhengeri where Northeast calm winds are predominant.

analysisPurpose: Evaluate model robustness and investigate the influence of parameter modifications.
Identify the most suitable offshore-wind development sites within the South African EEZ.
analysisTechnique: Weighted sum overlay with analytical hierarchy process criterion weighting
analysisMethodDescription: Capacity factor, ocean bathymetry, distance from the existing Eskom transmission grid, and distance to commercial harbours were resampled, reclassified to a 1–10 suitability scale, weighted using the analytical hierarchy process, and combined using the ArcGIS weighted sum overlay tool.
analysisKeyOutcome: Richards Bay, Kwa Dukuza, Durban, and Struis Bay were identified as suitable offshore-wind development regions.

analysisPurpose: Determine the distribution of wind speed on each site according to topography and identify suitable locations for wind projects.
analysisMethodDescription: Wind-resource mapping used wind data, obstacle and roughness information, SRTM topographic data, WAsP, and vertical extrapolation to 100 m.
analysisKeyOutcome: The authors state that selecting high-resource areas from the mapping can identify suitable locations for implementation of wind projects.

analysisPurpose: Assess monthly wind-speed variations and whether there will be continuity of service for permanent electricity production at the station.
analysisKeyOutcome: Wind-speed variation showed two peaks in March and June for N'Djamena and in April and July for Faya; the authors state that these months are expected to be the most productive in terms of energy.

analysisPurpose: To test annual energy production behaviour by varying wind-speed parameters and to test LCOE sensitivities by varying annual energy production around base-case values.
analysisTechnique: Variation of wind-speed and annual-energy-production parameters
analysisKeyOutcome: Deviation of the actual values of wind-speed and annual-energy-production parameters affects the techno-economic performance of the small wind turbines.

analysisPurpose: Assess wind potential at four locations in southern Algeria.
analysisTechnique: Weibull distribution fitting using the standard deviation method
analysisMethodDescription: The statistical study processed wind data collected every 3 hours over 5 years and used Weibull distribution parameters calculated at 10 m from the ground.

analysisPurpose: Characterize daily mean wind-speed distributions and estimate wind-energy parameters.
analysisTechnique: two-parameter Weibull distribution fitting using multiple parameter-estimation methods
analysisKeyOutcome: The Weibull distribution provided satisfactory modeling of daily mean wind-speed probability distributions, and the power density method generally had the largest correlation coefficient among the compared methods.

analysisPurpose: Determine statistically significant long-term changes in annual mean wind speed.
analysisMethodDescription: Annual mean wind-speed changes over 1981–2018 were assessed at the 95% significance level using the Mann-Kendall test implemented in MATLAB.
analysisKeyOutcome: Fifteen of 38 stations and three of 11 regions showed statistically significant long-term changes in annual mean wind speed.

analysisPurpose: prepare meteorological dataset
analysisMethodDescription: Deleted erroneous indices outside 0.015-1 and interpolated short gaps.
analysisKeyOutcome: About 2.3% of database readings were deleted or interpolated.

analysisPurpose: identify homogeneous radiation zones
analysisMethodDescription: Developed an optimal criterion and applied k-means clustering to station data.
analysisKeyOutcome: Relative sunshine duration produced nine zones.

analysisPurpose: assess hybrid calibration benefit
analysisMethodDescription: Evaluated ANN/SA against ANN, SVM, regression and other models.
analysisKeyOutcome: ANN/SA outperformed comparison models.

analysisPurpose: rank CSP sites and quantify potential
analysisTechnique: AHP-weighted GIS overlay and sensitivity analysis
analysisMethodDescription: Mapped unsuitable/suitable land and calculated regional theoretical CSP potential.
analysisKeyOutcome: Far North was especially suitable; standard potential 37,917.005 TWh/year.

analysisPurpose: Identify main daily solar-radiation profiles and associated sky conditions.
analysisMethodDescription: Applied Euclidean-distance hierarchical clustering with Ward aggregation in XLSTAT to hourly GSR diurnal cycles; selected five classes after inspection of the clustering tree.
analysisKeyOutcome: Five profiles ranging from bright to obscure days were identified and linked to cloud-type occurrences.

analysisPurpose: Identify high- and low-radiation seasons and their drivers.
analysisMethodDescription: Compared monthly global solar radiation with sunshine duration, temperature, precipitation, and cloudiness.
analysisKeyOutcome: DJF is bright and dry; JJAS is dark and rainy; MAM and ON are semi-illuminated transition periods.

analysisPurpose: assess output stability and curtailment
analysisMethodDescription: Varied thermal storage solar multiple and heater capacity.
analysisKeyOutcome: Bigger TES and smaller solar multiple reduced wind curtailment.

analysisPurpose: establish the national energy context
analysisMethodDescription: Summarized installed capacity generation mix electricity access and network indicators.
analysisKeyOutcome: Hydropower provided 92.7% of generation while electricity access remained below 50%.

analysisPurpose: characterize national wind potential and evidence quality
analysisMethodDescription: Compared CESEN broad-region estimates with SWERA mesoscale maps and meteorological evidence.
analysisKeyOutcome: Wind potential was estimated at 10000 MW but sparse low-height measurements limited accuracy.

analysisPurpose: identify promising development sites
analysisMethodDescription: Reviewed 10 m and 40 m measurements correlated with 25 years of NCEP data at five regions.
analysisKeyOutcome: Long-term mean speeds at 40 m ranged from 5.7 to 9.4 m/s and peaked in the hydro-poor dry season.

analysisPurpose: evaluate diversification plans
analysisMethodDescription: Compiled ongoing and planned wind geothermal and hydropower projects and commissioning targets.
analysisKeyOutcome: Eight wind farms totaling 1116 MW were planned and Adama I was operating by December 2012.

analysisPurpose: Identify spatially distributed theoretical run-of-river potential.
analysisTechnique: DEM-stream overlay, SWAT simulation, sensitivity analysis, and flow-duration curves
analysisMethodDescription: Sites required fifth-or-higher-order streams, at least 2% average bed gradient, and at least 500 m separation. SWAT was calibrated on sensitive parameters and validated against observed water yield.
analysisKeyOutcome: 107 potential sites were identified across nine streams in the watershed.

analysisPurpose: characterize adoption barriers
analysisMethodDescription: Grouped 75 barriers into economic/financial, technological, policy/regulatory, social/cultural, resource/geographic, market/industry, and institutional categories.
analysisKeyOutcome: Financial and policy-related barriers were most significant.

analysisPurpose: test ranking robustness
analysisMethodDescription: Varied each of seven criterion weights while proportionally adjusting the remainder and compared leading strategy ranks.
analysisKeyOutcome: Policy stability remained first under most variations; leading strategies were broadly stable.

analysisPurpose: Identify decision-making factors that motivate or constrain municipal renewable-energy development.
analysisTechnique: descriptive statistics and binary logistic regression
analysisMethodDescription: Survey responses were categorized with the Theory of Planned Behaviour and transition theory; ranked barriers and opportunity scales were modeled against stated project-development intention.
analysisKeyOutcome: Economic value motivates municipalities, while natural-vista concerns and external-support barriers significantly reduce stated development intention.

analysisPurpose: Identify system failures and policy needs that affect technology commercialisation.
analysisTechnique: sectoral system mapping and technology-maturity assessment
analysisMethodDescription: Analysed primary innovation drivers, knowledge creation/diffusion/exploitation, public–private partnerships, intellectual-property rights, international dimensions, and other systemic influences for each sector.
analysisKeyOutcome: The principal gaps are between demonstration and pre-commercial stages and between pre-commercial and supported commercialisation.

analysisPurpose: Identify reforms needed for a European transition to renewable electricity.
analysisMethodDescription: Specified carbon lock-in barriers across electricity generation, grids, storage, and demand response, then assessed existing and required policy responses.
analysisKeyOutcome: Policies should extend beyond generation to grid, storage, and demand measures and be integrated across Member States.

analysisPurpose: Guide policy priorities for renewable-project development.
analysisTechnique: quota-sampled questionnaire ratings and semi-structured interviews
analysisMethodDescription: Calculated mean, variance, and standard deviation for 18 barrier ratings and used interviews to contextualize the highest-ranked barriers.
analysisKeyOutcome: Grid capacity/connection, permits, land and water securement, and financing are the most critical barriers.

analysisPurpose: Develop actionable stakeholder-centred strategies for renewable-energy adoption.
analysisTechnique: literature review and comparative real-world case studies
analysisMethodDescription: Examined technical, financial, policy/regulatory, and socio-cultural barriers and the roles of governments, private entities, financial institutions, and local communities.
analysisKeyOutcome: Integrated, context-specific approaches coupling stable policy, finance innovation, capacity building, and community engagement are needed.

analysisPurpose: Objectively choose sufficient ensemble size.
analysisMethodDescription: Compared 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1000 ensemble members for six assimilated products using KGE and its components.
analysisKeyOutcome: Most products stabilised with 25 members; discharge and reservoir inflow required 100.

analysisPurpose: assess flow dependability for hydropower operation
analysisMethodDescription: Plots monthly discharge against exceedance probability.
analysisKeyOutcome: Classified 0–15% as high flow, 15–40% as moist, 40–60% as mid-range, 60–85% as dry, and 85–100% as low flow.

analysisPurpose: Identify suitable SHP dam sites across a large watershed.
analysisTechnique: AHP weighted overlay and semi-automatic spatial query
analysisMethodDescription: Ten thematic criteria were normalized, AHP weighted, and overlaid. A contour, stream-order, and suitability intersection was queried for valleys with stream order >3, width <200 m, elevation <400 m, and very high/high suitability.
analysisKeyOutcome: The suitability map and field validation support 18 feasible potential sites, while high-resolution DEM data would improve valley-width accuracy.

analysisPurpose: validate groundwater potential
analysisMethodDescription: Twenty VES measurements were interpreted manually and with WINRESIST to estimate aquifer thickness and resistivity.
analysisKeyOutcome: VES potential classes broadly corresponded to RS/GIS classes.

analysisPurpose: prepare groundwater-control inputs
analysisMethodDescription: Derived lithology, lineament density, slope, drainage density, and land-use/cover layers.
analysisKeyOutcome: Five thematic layers were prepared for integration.

analysisPurpose: delineate groundwater-potential zones
analysisMethodDescription: Reclassified thematic layers were weighted and overlaid in ArcGIS.
analysisKeyOutcome: Four zones were mapped; high-to-moderate coverage was 52%.

analysisPurpose: identify feasible SHP sites
analysisTechnique: GIS head slope and Q92 filtering
analysisMethodDescription: Screened 58 points using slope at least 2% and head at least 10 m.
analysisKeyOutcome: Eleven sites had 393.849–16038.194 kW potential.

analysisPurpose: characterize annual flow availability
analysisMethodDescription: Constructed primary and residual-flow-adjusted secondary curves from daily flow observations.
analysisKeyOutcome: Average available flow was 21.4 m3/s at 40.5% exceedance; minimum available flow was 2.97 m3/s.

analysisPurpose: characterize ability to sustain rated output
analysisMethodDescription: Calculated plant output across available flows using turbine-specific efficiency curves.
analysisKeyOutcome: Average-flow configurations lose output during reduced dry-season flows.

analysisPurpose: assess head sensitivity
analysisMethodDescription: Evaluated rated output, annual energy, and capacity factor over a medium range of heads.
analysisKeyOutcome: Rated output and annual energy increased with head.

analysisPurpose: identify preliminary SHP locations
analysisMethodDescription: Overlaid water areas and waterlines with national and administrative maps.
analysisKeyOutcome: Highlighted opportunities in Borno Niger Edo Anambra and Jigawa.

analysisPurpose: compare regional opportunities
analysisMethodDescription: Summarized inland-water and potential-site patterns across six zones.
analysisKeyOutcome: North-East had 151 potential small-dam sites and North-West 95.

analysisPurpose: prioritize accessible water-related locations
analysisTechnique: ring buffers and inverse distance weighting
analysisMethodDescription: Used 200 m to 5 km waterbody buffers and IDW interpolation to visualize potential areas.
analysisKeyOutcome: Generated maps for dam schemes and lower-storage SHP schemes.

analysisPurpose: prepare SHP screening inputs
analysisMethodDescription: Derived DEM elevation slope drainage and catchment parameters.
analysisKeyOutcome: Generated 148 candidate drainage-network points.

analysisPurpose: estimate reliable SHP power
analysisMethodDescription: Combined design discharge and available head for potential calculation.
analysisKeyOutcome: Eighteen sites met criteria and yielded 677.485–7622.877 kW.

analysisPurpose: select a donor watershed
analysisMethodDescription: Compared Gumera and Upper Rib with Beshilo using catchment area, rainfall, topography, land use, and soil.
analysisKeyOutcome: Gumera was the closest hydrologically similar gauged catchment.

analysisPurpose: identify influential streamflow controls
analysisMethodDescription: Screened runoff soil groundwater vegetation and channel parameters before calibration.
analysisKeyOutcome: Twelve parameters were identified as significantly influencing catchment streamflow.

analysisPurpose: locate hydropower sites
analysisMethodDescription: Required third-order or higher streams, at least 2000 accumulated cells, at least 20 m head, and at least 1 km spacing; also considered construction and sediment suitability.
analysisKeyOutcome: Nine sites were retained: three upstream three midstream and three downstream.

analysisPurpose: characterize dependable water availability
analysisMethodDescription: Ranked simulated daily flows at each site to derive Q90 Q75 and Q50.
analysisKeyOutcome: Sites 1 and 2 had the highest Q90 discharge and all sites had year-round monthly flow.

analysisPurpose: remove unsuitable PHES locations
analysisMethodDescription: Excluded protected areas settlements steep slopes and unsuitable reservoir pairs.
analysisKeyOutcome: Protected areas and slopes above 5% were excluded.

analysisPurpose: rank PHES decision factors
analysisMethodDescription: Weighted head H/D slope TWI lineaments and grid road and river proximity.
analysisKeyOutcome: Head was highest at 29.8% and H/D second at 17.9%.

analysisPurpose: identify optimal PHES zones
analysisMethodDescription: Reclassified and overlaid eight rasterized thematic layers around seven reservoirs.
analysisKeyOutcome: Very high suitability covered 2.6 km2 or 0.17% of analyzed area.

analysisPurpose: identify influential calibration parameters
analysisMethodDescription: Identified eight sensitive parameters affecting watershed streamflow.
analysisKeyOutcome: Eight parameters significantly influenced simulated streamflow.

analysisPurpose: identify candidate run-of-river sites
analysisMethodDescription: Screened fourth- and higher-order streams by head and separation distance.
analysisKeyOutcome: Results state 33 sites with at least 20 m head and 500 m separation; conclusion reports 20 sites using 10 m and 1000 m criteria.

analysisPurpose: estimate theoretical generation
analysisMethodDescription: Ranked annual runoff and calculated potential at 50% 75% and 90% dependable flows.
analysisKeyOutcome: Reported aggregate power totals conflict between results and conclusion.

analysisPurpose: identify a suitable GERD filling duration
analysisMethodDescription: Compared energy loss and downstream-flow loss for ten filling durations under both release policies.
analysisKeyOutcome: Approximately 4–5 years minimized energy loss; periods longer than 6–7 years degraded performance.

analysisPurpose: identify run-of-river candidates
analysisMethodDescription: Segmented second-order and higher streams at 500 m intervals, retained scheme lengths up to 3 km, and selected heads of at least 20 m.
analysisKeyOutcome: 103 candidate sites with heads from 20 to 81 m were identified.

analysisPurpose: identify dominant streamflow parameters
analysisMethodDescription: Ranked parameters using absolute t-statistics and P-values.
analysisKeyOutcome: SCS curve number was most sensitive; channel conductivity and roughness and soil/runoff parameters were also dominant.

analysisPurpose: quantify dependable flow and theoretical power
analysisTechnique: flow-duration curves and physical power calculation
analysisMethodDescription: Ranked 28 years of daily simulated flows and combined Q50, Q75, and Q90 with GIS-derived head.
analysisKeyOutcome: Total potential was 183.16, 125.96, and 33.03 MW at 50%, 75%, and 90% exceedance.

analysisPurpose: rank sites for implementation
analysisMethodDescription: Weighted power, discharge, head, scheme length, and accessibility and linearly combined their raster maps.
analysisKeyOutcome: Weights were 0.43, 0.27, 0.17, 0.09, and 0.05 for power, discharge, head, scheme length, and accessibility.

analysisPurpose: describe study-area climate
analysisMethodDescription: Summarized rainfall and temperature observations from five stations.
analysisKeyOutcome: Mean annual rainfall was 1389 mm and annual mean temperature was 19.1 °C.

analysisPurpose: Identify potential Furfuro River hydropower sites and assess the reliability of elevation-derived head data.
analysisTechnique: DEM-derived stream network and head analysis with Google Earth and handheld-GPS elevation comparison
analysisMethodDescription: The 12.5 m DEM generated stream order and candidate reaches; head screening applied minimum-head, spacing, and environmental constraints, then compared four Google Earth and GPS head-drop measurements.
analysisKeyOutcome: Four potential sites on fourth- and fifth-order reaches met the reported head-screening criteria; Google Earth/GPS head comparison achieved R² 0.994 and NSE 0.997.

analysisPurpose: Compare hydroelectric potential of Chemoga, Huluka, and Wabe under flow variability.
analysisTechnique: Weibull flow-duration curve, QGIS topographic analysis, net-head equation, and cross-flow turbine power equation
analysisMethodDescription: Ten-year daily flow records were converted to FDCs and grouped into five flow bands. QGIS/GPS Visualizer topography informed net-head assessment; a fixed 20 m net head and 80% cross-flow efficiency yielded theoretical outputs.
analysisKeyOutcome: Chemoga has highest high/moist/mid-range output; Wabe has highest dry and low-flow output and the largest elevation change per 11.1 km.

analysisPurpose: Identify, quantify, and configure a feasible cascade.
analysisTechnique: remote sensing, SWAT-CUP/SUFI-2, FDC, PDC, and turbine chart
analysisKeyOutcome: Nine sites combine for 7.89 MW firm power; HP1, HP4, and HP7 are the recommended 55.72 GWh/year cascade.

analysisPurpose: identify feasible small-hydropower sites
analysisMethodDescription: Applied stream orders 3–4, head of at least 10 m, maximum stream reach of 120 m, and at least 1000 m site spacing.
analysisKeyOutcome: Reduced 30 possible locations to six dam and three run-of-river sites.

analysisPurpose: support ungauged-basin streamflow simulation
analysisMethodDescription: Adjusted runoff, soil-water, groundwater, and channel parameters and transferred calibrated behavior from the similar Bamboi catchment.
analysisKeyOutcome: The calibrated model achieved good or very good performance across reported criteria.

analysisPurpose: estimate dependable discharge
analysisMethodDescription: Constructed monthly FDCs from dry-year modeled flows for each of nine sites.
analysisKeyOutcome: Q90 values ranged from 1.23 to 21.34 m3/s across dam sites and 1.6 to 14.20 m3/s across run-of-river sites.

analysisPurpose: estimate firm power and energy
analysisMethodDescription: Converted each site's flow-duration curve to power using head and 75% efficiency.
analysisKeyOutcome: Nine sites jointly offered at least 38.9 GWh annually; the average site yielded 844 kW and 4.32 GWh.

analysisPurpose: Identify feasible sites and a cascade.
analysisTechnique: GIS screening, SWAT, FDC/PDC, power calculation, storage and turbine screening
analysisKeyOutcome: Ten sites were identified; HP1, HP3 and HP7 form a recommended 483.4 GWh/year cascade.

analysisPurpose: Quantify hydrological-extreme impacts on hydropower performance and an electricity-use proxy.
analysisMethodDescription: Discharge deviations defined relative to each gauge’s long-run monthly mean; dry and wet extremes were below the fifth and above the 95th percentile, respectively.
analysisKeyOutcome: Dry extremes reduced hydropower capacity factor and urban nighttime-light radiance.

analysisPurpose: Identify drivers of China’s low-carbon power transition.
analysisTechnique: single-factor sensitivity and multi-factor scenario analysis
analysisMethodDescription: Nonseasonal drivers were fitted with adjusted quadratic trends and seasonal drivers with month-specific adjusted linear trends; individual share predictions were normalized to sum to one.
analysisKeyOutcome: Transmission expansion mainly benefits hydropower; rapid demand, urbanization, and industrial upgrading raise the thermal-power share.

analysisPurpose: assess forecast reliability
analysisMethodDescription: Compared PICP and PINW for four GPRE-containing models.
analysisKeyOutcome: CNNE-MUPE-GPRE produced the highest coverage and narrowest intervals; uncertainty increased with horizon.

analysisPurpose: identify influential watershed-model parameters
analysisMethodDescription: Varied six calibrated parameters by ±10%, ±20%, ±25%, and ±50% and assessed discharge deviation.
analysisKeyOutcome: Soil evaporation compensation factor was most sensitive; channel Manning coefficient and baseflow recession alpha were least sensitive.

analysisPurpose: identify candidate run-of-river sites
analysisMethodDescription: Applied stream order, flow accumulation, head, and spacing criteria to the generated stream network.
analysisKeyOutcome: Identified 33 candidate sites in the 147 km2 basin.

analysisPurpose: identify influential flow controls
analysisMethodDescription: Ranked ten streamflow parameters by P-value after fitting their ranges.
analysisKeyOutcome: Surface-runoff lag and soil hydraulic parameters ranked most sensitive.

analysisPurpose: characterize hydrological support for SHP development
analysisMethodDescription: Summarized modeled streamflow, baseflow, runoff, recharge, percolation, and evapotranspiration relative to precipitation.
analysisKeyOutcome: Streamflow/precipitation was 0.39, surface-runoff/total-flow 0.52, and ET/precipitation 0.56.

analysisPurpose: map relative hydropower suitability
analysisMethodDescription: Reclassified equal-resolution DEM, slope, flow direction, land cover, soil, rainfall, ET, and water-yield layers into four weighted classes.
analysisKeyOutcome: Produced least feasible, moderately suitable, feasible, and optimum suitable zones; outlet areas were optimum.

analysisPurpose: identify possible small-hydropower sites
analysisMethodDescription: Used suitability zones, slope, flow direction, and stream accumulation to locate tentative projects.
analysisKeyOutcome: Ten tentative sites were mapped: seven upstream and three near the outlet.

analysisPurpose: Reduce the time and labor needed to survey inaccessible potential sites.
analysisTechnique: fuzzy image clustering and knowledge-based interpretation
analysisMethodDescription: Satellite images were first segmented and classified, then interpreted with water-resource, vegetation, habitation, settlement, and snow information for site selection.
analysisKeyOutcome: Demonstrated comprehensive satellite-derived feature mapping for small-hydropower site identification.

analysisPurpose: Identify barriers and sustainability factors for large RoR development.
analysisTechnique: document review, field visits, expert interviews, and local group discussions
analysisMethodDescription: Assessed social, environmental, economic, policy, topographic/geological, and security indicators; compared reservoir and run-of-river contexts.
analysisKeyOutcome: Security, public participation, local employment, policy/clearance delay, capital cost, muck disposal, diverted-reach length, and aquatic impacts are critical RoR factors.

analysisPurpose: identify high- and low-rainfall areas
analysisTechnique: mean, standard deviation, standard error, median, minimum, and maximum
analysisMethodDescription: Summarized the 1931–2022 rainfall record for 36 states or meteorological subdivisions.
analysisKeyOutcome: Arunachal Pradesh, Coastal Karnataka, Lakshadweep, Kerala, and Konkan-Goa had the highest mean rainfall; western Rajasthan and western Uttar Pradesh had the lowest.

analysisPurpose: examine correspondence between rainfall and existing hydro development
analysisMethodDescription: Compared mean rainfall with installed hydro energy capacity for 21 states.
analysisKeyOutcome: Arunachal Pradesh combined the largest reported capacity with the highest state mean rainfall in the comparison, but rainfall and capacity did not align uniformly across states.

analysisPurpose: identify states with extensive hydropower-supporting water resources
analysisMethodDescription: Examined major river-basin membership and state shares of basin area.
analysisKeyOutcome: Maharashtra, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, and Gujarat were highlighted for large basin areas and substantial water resources.

analysisPurpose: screen regions for hydropower development
analysisMethodDescription: Assigned high moderate or low hydropower-potential labels to eight regions using average annual rainfall ranges.
analysisKeyOutcome: Western Ghats, Northeast India, and the Himalayan region were classified as high potential.

analysisPurpose: identify input-output relationships
analysisMethodDescription: Compared pairwise associations among ten inputs and generation capacity.
analysisKeyOutcome: System water volume had the strongest positive association; transmission spurline cost was next; total dollar per kW had the strongest negative association.

analysisPurpose: rank predictors of hydropower capacity
analysisMethodDescription: Measured distributional output changes caused by fixing each input variable.
analysisKeyOutcome: System water volume was most sensitive, followed by transmission spurline cost and total dollar per kW; hydraulic head showed lesser sensitivity.

analysisPurpose: Interpret input influence on hydropower generation.
analysisTechnique: correlation matrix and PAWN sensitivity index
analysisMethodDescription: Correlation characterized direction and strength of feature relationships; sensitivity used minimum, maximum, mean, median, and coefficient-of-variation PAWN-index summaries.
analysisKeyOutcome: System water volume and total dollars per kilowatt were most sensitive; hydraulic head had strong positive correlation, whereas upper reservoir coordinates were negligible.

analysisPurpose: Assess weather-input relationships and identify a suitable temporal scale for prediction.
analysisMethodDescription: Examined pairwise collinearity and relations of rainfall stations to power generation at monthly and quarterly scales.
analysisKeyOutcome: Monthly rainfall had little same-month correlation with generation; rainfall at Alupola was weakest, and quarterly inputs yielded better models.

analysisPurpose: identify adoption barriers and motives
analysisMethodDescription: Grouped evidence into financial/economic, socio-political/regulatory/environmental, and behavioral/psychological clusters.
analysisKeyOutcome: Regulatory protection of fossil incumbents, unstable policy, weak participation, information and skill gaps, complexity, trust, privacy, and reliability concerns were prominent barriers.

analysisPurpose: identify appropriate policy responses
analysisMethodDescription: Mapped barriers to perceived usefulness, ease of use, relative advantage, compatibility, and complexity, then linked them to economic and non-economic measures.
analysisKeyOutcome: Recommended financial support where needed alongside regulatory reform, streamlined permissions, information campaigns, education, training, capacity building, privacy rules, and prosumer-enabling legislation.

analysisPurpose: explain differing initiative outcomes
analysisMethodDescription: Classified success factors under strategic, institutional, and physical conditions and their cultural, organizational, personal, political, legal, economic, and socio-cultural capacities.
analysisKeyOutcome: Leadership, knowledge, supportive authorities, sound regulation, finance, learning capacity, renewable resources, land, and technological development condition project success.

analysisPurpose: characterize citizen-led transition pathways
analysisMethodDescription: Reviewed individual and collective prosumption, energy communities, and renewable-energy cooperatives in rural settings.
analysisKeyOutcome: Energy communities and cooperatives are expanding forms of rural renewable-energy penetration and can increase participation and social acceptance.

analysisPurpose: map monthly radiation estimates
analysisKeyOutcome: Monthly solar-radiation maps created across Iran.

analysisPurpose: compare RES environmental trade-offs
analysisMethodDescription: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats framework applied to RES technologies.
